title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnets
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Physics
summary: What a magnetic field is and how to draw it, how magnetic fields push and pull on each other, and how to make, use and investigate the strength of an electromagnet.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe a **magnetic field**: the region around a magnet where it exerts a force, and understand that a magnet's field exerts a force on other magnetic fields (so magnets attract or repel). (8Pe.01)
Describe how to **make an electromagnet**, and know that electromagnets have **many uses**. (8Pe.02)
**Investigate the factors** that change the strength of an electromagnet: number of turns, current and core. (8Pe.03)

Thinking and Working Scientifically used on this page: planning an investigation with variables (8TWSp.04), risk assessment (8TWSp.05), repeat readings (8TWSc.03), anomalous results and trends (8TWSa.02), drawing graphs and conclusions (8TWSa.03, 8TWSa.05).

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: magnetic material
مادة مغناطيسية — a material attracted by a magnet: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt
pole
قطب — an end of a magnet where the force is strongest: north (N) or south (S)
magnetic field
المجال المغناطيسي — the region around a magnet where it exerts a force on magnetic materials and other magnets
field line
خط المجال — a line showing the direction of the magnetic field; drawn from N to S
plotting compass
بوصلة صغيرة — a small compass used to find the direction of a magnetic field
electromagnet
مغناطيس كهربائي — a coil of wire that becomes a magnet when an electric current flows through it
coil
ملف — wire wound round and round in many turns
core
القلب — the material inside the coil, usually iron
current
التيار الكهربائي — the flow of electric charge round a circuit, measured in amperes (A)
permanent magnet
مغناطيس دائم — a magnet that keeps its magnetism all the time, e.g. a steel bar magnet

blocks.text: 2. Magnets — a quick reminder

items: Every magnet has a **north pole (N)** and a **south pole (S)**. The forces are strongest at the poles.
**Like poles repel** (N–N or S–S push apart). **Unlike poles attract** (N–S pull together).
Magnets attract **magnetic materials**: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Most metals (copper, aluminium, gold) are **not** magnetic.
Only a magnet can **repel** another magnet — so repulsion is the true test of whether an object is a magnet. A piece of iron is attracted by both poles.

blocks.text: 3. What is a magnetic field?

A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where it exerts a force on magnetic materials and on other magnets. You cannot see a magnetic field, but you can show its shape with **iron filings** or with **plotting compasses**. We draw it with **magnetic field lines**.

blocks.caption: The magnetic field around a bar magnet. Field lines leave the north pole and go round to the south pole. They are closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest.

blocks.title: Rules for field lines
items: Field lines go **from the north pole to the south pole** (outside the magnet). The arrow shows the direction a plotting compass's north end would point.
The field is **strongest where the lines are closest together** — at the poles.
Field lines **never cross** each other.
The field surrounds the magnet in **all directions** (in three dimensions, not just on the paper).

blocks.text: **Plotting the field with a compass:**

items: Put the bar magnet in the middle of a sheet of paper and draw round it. Label N and S.
Place a small plotting compass near the north pole. Mark a dot at each end of the compass needle.
Move the compass so that its tail is on the dot you just made at its head. Mark a new dot at the head.
Repeat until you reach the south pole (or the edge of the paper). Join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow pointing away from N.
Start again at a different point near the north pole to draw more field lines.

blocks.text: **Iron filings** are quicker: place paper over the magnet, sprinkle filings and tap gently. The filings line up along the field lines and crowd together at the poles. But filings do **not** show the **direction** of the field — a compass does.
4. Fields acting on other fields
A magnetic field exerts a force on **other magnetic fields**. When two magnets come close, their fields overlap and combine. This is why magnets attract or repel, even without touching.

blocks.caption: Unlike poles (N facing S): field lines go straight across from N to S. The magnets attract.
Like poles (N facing N): field lines push away from each other. At the point marked × the two fields cancel (a neutral point). The magnets repel.

blocks.text: The same idea explains why a compass works: the compass needle is a tiny magnet, and the Earth's magnetic field exerts a force on its field and turns it to point north. (You will study the Earth's field in another lesson.)
5. Electromagnets

When an **electric current** flows through a wire, it makes a **magnetic field** around the wire. The field of a straight wire is weak, but if the wire is wound into a **coil**, the fields of all the turns add together. Putting an **iron core** inside the coil makes the field much stronger. This is an **electromagnet**.

blocks.text: **How to make an electromagnet:**

items: Take a length of **insulated** copper wire (the plastic coating stops the current taking a short cut between the turns).
Wind it tightly round an **iron** nail (the core) many times, always in the **same direction**.
Connect the two ends of the wire to a **cell** (or low-voltage power supply) and a **switch**.
Close the switch: current flows, and the nail becomes a magnet that can pick up paper clips.
Open the switch: the current stops, the magnetism disappears and the paper clips drop.

blocks.text: The field of an electromagnet has the **same shape as a bar magnet's field**, with a N pole at one end of the coil and a S pole at the other. **Reversing the current** (turning the cell round) **swaps the poles**.

rows: **yes** — change the current or the number of turns

blocks.text: **Why iron and not steel for the core?** Iron becomes strongly magnetised while the current flows and **loses its magnetism** as soon as the current stops. Steel would stay magnetised (it would become a permanent magnet), so the electromagnet could not be switched off properly.
6. Uses of electromagnets
Electromagnets are used wherever we need a magnet that can be **switched on and off** or **controlled**:

rows: lifts heavy iron and steel scrap (such as old cars), then drops it when the current is switched off
separates steel cans (magnetic) from aluminium cans (not magnetic)
holds a door shut while the current flows; releases it when a card is accepted or the power is switched off
the electromagnet pulls an iron arm that hits the bell, switching itself on and off rapidly
a small current in an electromagnet switches on a separate circuit with a large current, e.g. a car's starter motor
an electromagnet in the speaker is pushed and pulled by a permanent magnet, making the cone vibrate to make sound
very strong electromagnets are used to make images of the inside of the body
electromagnets lift the train above the track and push it along, so there is no friction with the rails

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية
items: المجال المغناطيسي = المنطقة حوالين المغناطيس اللي بيأثر فيها بقوة. خطوطه بتطلع من الشمال (N) وتدخل في الجنوب (S)، وأقوى مكان عند الأقطاب لأن الخطوط متقاربة.
المغناطيس الكهربائي = سلك معزول ملفوف لفّات كتير حوالين قلب حديد ومتوصل ببطارية. لما التيار يمشي يبقى مغناطيس، ولما يقف يبطل.
عشان تقوّيه: زوّد عدد اللفات، أو زوّد التيار، أو استخدم قلب حديد.

blocks.text: 7. Factors that change the strength of an electromagnet

rows: each turn adds its own magnetic field
**bigger current** (e.g. more cells in series / higher voltage)
a bigger current makes a stronger field around every turn
an **iron** core (much stronger than no core / air, or a non-magnetic core such as wood, plastic, copper or aluminium)
the iron becomes magnetised and adds its own strong field

blocks.text: **Measuring strength.** The usual method is to count how many identical paper clips the electromagnet can pick up (or how long a chain it holds). Other methods: measure the mass of iron filings it lifts, or the distance from which it attracts a paper clip.
8. Planning the investigation
**Question:** How does the number of turns on the coil affect the strength of an electromagnet?

rows: number of paper clips picked up
the current (same cell / same power-supply setting), the same iron nail (core), the same type and size of paper clips, the same wire, the same way of lowering the nail onto the clips

blocks.text: **Prediction** (using scientific knowledge): the more turns, the more paper clips will be picked up, because each turn adds to the magnetic field.
**Method:** wind 10 turns, switch on, lower the nail into a pile of clips, lift it, count the clips, switch off. Repeat three times and calculate a mean. Then wind more turns and repeat.

**Risk assessment:** the wire can get **hot** when the current flows, especially with a short wire and a large current. Control the risk: use a low-voltage supply or a single cell, switch off between readings and do not hold the coil while it is switched on. Never connect a bare wire straight across a cell (short circuit).

**Reliability:** repeat each reading at least three times. If the repeats are close together, the results are reliable. If one repeat is very different (anomalous), check it and leave it out of the mean.

**Accuracy and precision:** counting paper clips only gives whole numbers, so small changes in strength may not be noticed. A more precise method is to measure the force needed to pull a piece of iron off the electromagnet with a newton meter, or to weigh the iron filings it lifts.

**Presenting results:** number of turns is a continuous number variable, so plot a **line graph** with the number of turns on the x-axis and the number of clips on the y-axis. (If the independent variable were the type of core — iron, steel, wood — you would use a **bar chart**, because it is a category.)

blocks.text: **Conclusion:** as the number of turns increases, the number of paper clips picked up increases — the electromagnet gets stronger. 9. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Describe what is meant by a magnetic field. [1] Describe how a plotting compass can be used to show the direction of the field around a bar magnet. [2]

items: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet feels a force (1).
Place the compass near the magnet and mark where the needle points; move the compass along in that direction, marking dots, and join them (1).
The compass needle's north end points in the direction of the field — away from N and towards S (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Two bar magnets are placed end to end. The field lines between them go straight across the gap from one magnet to the other. Do the magnets attract or repel? Explain. [2]

items: They **attract** (1).
Field lines going straight across the gap show a north pole facing a south pole; unlike poles attract (1).
**Common mistake:** thinking lines across the gap mean the fields are fighting. When like poles face each other, the lines bend away and there is a neutral point with no field.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — A scrapyard uses an electromagnet on a crane, not a permanent magnet. Give two reasons. [2]

items: The electromagnet can be **switched off**, so the crane can **drop** the scrap where it is needed (1).
Its strength can be **changed** (by changing the current) to suit the load (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Aya wants to find out whether the size of the current affects the strength of an electromagnet. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables. [3]

items: Independent variable: the **current** (1).
Dependent variable: the **number of paper clips** picked up (or another measure of strength) (1).
Control variables, any two: number of turns, the core (same nail), size/type of paper clips, the wire (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Use the graph in section 8. (a) Estimate how many paper clips 25 turns would pick up. [1] (b) A student says "the line shows that 100 turns would pick up about 35 clips". Comment on this claim. [1]

items: (a) Read up from 25 turns to the line, then across: about **8 or 9** clips (accept 8–9).

(b) 100 turns is far **outside the range tested** (10–50). We cannot be sure the pattern continues — for example, the core might not keep getting stronger at the same rate — so this prediction may not be accurate; it should be tested.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Explain why an electromagnet used in a door lock has a core made of **iron** and not **steel**. [2]

items: Iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off (1).
Steel would stay magnetised, so the lock would not release when the current stops (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Drawing field lines from **S to N**, or with no arrows. Outside the magnet they go **N → S**.
Drawing field lines that **cross** or that do not touch the poles.
Saying a magnetic field is "the magnet's force" without saying it is the **region around the magnet**.
Saying "more electricity" or "more power". Say **more current** (or more cells / a higher voltage).
Saying "use a bigger nail" as the main factor. The three factors to learn are **number of turns, current and core material**.
Forgetting that the wire must be **insulated**.
In investigations: changing two variables at once (e.g. more turns **and** more cells) — then you cannot tell which one caused the change.
Choosing a bar chart for continuous data such as number of turns or current. Use a **line graph**.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Draw or complete** field lines around a bar magnet, with arrows; or **plot** the field from compass positions.
**Mark** where the field is strongest (where lines are closest, at the poles).
**Predict** whether two magnets attract or repel from their poles or field patterns.
**Label** a diagram of an electromagnet (coil, core, cell, switch) and **describe** how to make one.
**Name** factors that make an electromagnet stronger; **identify** variables in an investigation; **suggest** a risk and how to control it.
**Interpret results:** find an anomalous result, describe the trend, draw or read a line graph, make a prediction within the range, and say why a prediction outside the range may not be reliable.
**Give a use** of an electromagnet and explain why an electromagnet is better than a permanent magnet for that job.

questions.e: A magnetic field is the **region around a magnet** where a force acts on magnetic materials and on other magnets.

questions.q: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do the magnetic field lines point?
c: from the south pole to the north pole
from the middle of the magnet outwards
from the north pole to the south pole
questions.e: Field lines are drawn from the **north pole to the south pole** outside the magnet. This is the direction the north end of a plotting compass points.

questions.q: At which point, A, B, C or D, is the magnetic field strongest? [1]
questions.e: The field is strongest where the field lines are **closest together** — near the poles. Point **A** is right next to the north pole. B and D are far from the magnet and C is beside the middle of the magnet, where the field is weaker.
questions.p:
Question 3
The diagram shows the magnetic field around a bar magnet.

questions.q: Which arrangement of two bar magnets will **attract** each other?
questions.e: Unlike poles (N and S) attract; like poles (N–N or S–S) repel.

questions.q: Name the metal that is used for the core of an electromagnet so that it can be switched off. [1]
questions.e: **Iron**. It becomes strongly magnetised while the current flows and loses its magnetism when the current stops. (Steel would stay magnetised.)

questions.q: Describe how to make an electromagnet that can pick up paper clips. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: wind/coil (insulated) wire around a core. 1 mark: the core is iron (e.g. an iron nail). 1 mark: connect the ends of the coil to a cell/battery/power supply (with a switch) so that a current flows. Accept a correctly labelled diagram. Do not accept 'rub the nail with a magnet' (that makes a permanent magnet).
questions.e: Wind a length of **insulated wire** many times round a core (1). Use an **iron** nail as the core (1). Connect the two ends of the wire to a **cell** and a switch, so that a **current** flows when the switch is closed (1).

questions.q: Which change would make an electromagnet **weaker**?
questions.e: Fewer turns of wire make a **weaker** electromagnet. A bigger current, an iron core and an extra cell (which increases the current) all make it **stronger**.

questions.q: Why is an electromagnet, not a permanent magnet, used on a scrapyard crane?
c: It can be switched off to drop the scrap.
questions.e: The crane must **let go** of the scrap. An electromagnet loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the scrap drops. Electromagnets need electricity, and no magnet attracts aluminium.

questions.q: (a) At which current did Omar get an anomalous result? [1]
questions.e: The other results go up by 3 clips for every 0.5 A: 3, 6, …, 12, 15. At **1.5 A** we expect about 9 clips, but Omar got 13 — more than at 2.0 A. This result does not fit the pattern, so it is anomalous.
questions.p:
Question 9
Omar investigates how the current affects the strength of an electromagnet. He counts the paper clips it picks up.
Current / A | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | 2.5
Number of paper clips | 3 | 6 | 13 | 12 | 15

questions.q: (b) Name the **independent** variable in Omar's investigation. [1]
questions.e: The independent variable is the one Omar **changes**: the **current**. (The number of paper clips is the dependent variable.)
questions.p:
Question 9
Omar investigates how the current affects the strength of an electromagnet. He counts the paper clips it picks up.
Current / A | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | 2.5
Number of paper clips | 3 | 6 | 13 | 12 | 15

questions.q: (c) Which of these must Omar keep the same (a control variable)?
c: the number of paper clips picked up
the number of turns on the coil
questions.e: The **number of turns** affects the strength, so it must be kept the same for a fair test. The current is the independent variable and the number of clips is the dependent variable.

questions.q: (d) Use the pattern in the results to predict how many paper clips the electromagnet would pick up with a current of 3.0 A. [1]
questions.e: Ignoring the anomaly, the number of clips goes up by 3 for every 0.5 A: 3, 6, (9), 12, 15. So at 3.0 A: 15 + 3 = **18** clips. (Accept 17–19.)
questions.p:

questions.q: (e) Give **one** risk in Omar's experiment and say how he can reduce it. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: a correct hazard — the wire/coil gets hot (could burn) / a short circuit / heavy weights falling (if heavy objects are lifted). 1 mark: a matching control — use a low current/voltage, switch off between readings, do not touch the coil while it is on, do not leave it switched on. The control must match the risk.
questions.e: Risk: with a large current the **wire gets hot** and could burn his fingers (1). Control: **switch off** between readings / use a low voltage / do not touch the coil while the current is on (1).

questions.q: Two electromagnets, X and Y, are identical except that X has 40 turns and Y has 20 turns. Predict which one will pick up more paper clips and explain your prediction. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: X (the one with 40 turns). 1 mark: more turns give a stronger magnetic field / each turn adds to the field. Do not accept 'X is bigger'.
questions.e: **X** will pick up more clips (1), because it has **more turns** of wire, and more turns make a **stronger magnetic field** (each turn adds its own field) (1).

blocks.title: Remember
items: A magnetic field is the **region around a magnet** where it exerts a force on magnetic materials and other magnets.
Field lines go **N → S** outside the magnet, never cross, and are closest (field strongest) at the poles.
Magnetic fields exert forces on each other: unlike poles attract, like poles repel.
Electromagnet = coil of **insulated wire** round an **iron core**, with a **current** flowing. Switch off → no magnetism.
Stronger electromagnet: **more turns**, **bigger current**, **iron core**.
Uses: scrapyard cranes, recycling, door locks, bells, relays, loudspeakers, MRI scanners, maglev trains.
